title.rendered: Outsourcing operators seek reforms to position Nigeria globally

content.rendered:
Nigeria’s outsourcing industry is pushing for faster workforce development and clearer regulatory standards as operators seek to position the country as a competitive destination for global business services.

Speaking at the 2026 Outsourcing Expo organised by the Association of Outsourcing Professionals of Nigeria in Lagos, industry leaders said the country’s youthful population offers a strong advantage in the global outsourcing market but cautioned that weak standards and compliance shortcomings could hinder growth.

The sector, they said, must move beyond being viewed as a cost-cutting solution and develop into a knowledge-driven export industry built around talent, technology and trust.

Delivering the keynote address at the event themed ‘Strengthening Nigeria’s Outsourcing Ecosystem for Global Competitiveness’, Chairman of Phillips Group, Foluso Phillips, said Nigeria’s biggest competitive advantage lies in developing its people.

“History will remember this decade as the period when the world’s most valuable resources were no longer oil, gold or even land, but talent,” Phillips told stakeholders at the summit.

The executive said outsourcing has evolved beyond reducing operational costs, with global demand increasingly driven by artificial intelligence services, cybersecurity, cloud engineering, financial analytics, software development and other specialised services.

“Outsourcing has never been about doing work. It has always been about multiplying your ability. It is a people strategy. It is a talent strategy,” he said.

Phillips said Nigeria’s demographic advantage must be matched with deliberate investment in skills, citing the growing importance of artificial intelligence and digital capabilities in the future of work.

According to him, while Nigeria has a large youthful workforce, employers continue to face difficulties finding workers with the skills required for emerging roles.

“That is not simply a demographic issue. It is an economic issue. It is a productivity issue. It is a competitiveness issue,” he said.

The industry veteran warned that countries that fail to reskill their workforce risk losing opportunities as companies globally rethink their outsourcing partnerships.

“The real danger is not artificial intelligence. The real danger is remaining artificially ignorant,” Phillips said, arguing that professionals who effectively use AI would gain an advantage over those who do not.

During a panel session titled Regulatory Excellence and ESG: Building a Sustainable Outsourcing Ecosystem, industry executives identified the absence of a clear regulatory framework as one of the biggest challenges facing Nigeria’s outsourcing sector.

Group Head, Human Resources at Sahara Group Ltd, Emilomo Arorote, said the industry currently lacks clear standards defining how outsourcing companies should operate, train workers and manage compliance.

“There is an absence of regulation for the outsourcing sector as of today. There is no clear structure or framework guiding how we approach outsourcing. There is a lot of ambiguity around it,” Arorote said.

She further noted that companies currently rely on identifying reputable outsourcing providers through experience because there are no industry-wide benchmarks separating professional operators from companies focused only on commercial gains.

Arorote said clearer standards are needed around training, employee management, compliance requirements and data protection, particularly as outsourcing arrangements involve thousands of workers handling sensitive business information.

“We are dealing with human beings. We are dealing with people’s careers and lives, and so it is important that there is structure around employment practices,” she said.

She also argued that employee welfare should become a bigger part of environmental, social and governance considerations within the sector: “ESG is not just about environmental issues or compliance checks. Employee welfare is a critical part of ESG, and that is becoming increasingly important globally.”

CEO of Regenerative Futures, Bobby Varanasi, said outsourcing companies should view regulation and compliance as a growth opportunity rather than a burden, noting that global outsourcing clients increasingly assess providers based on their ability to protect confidential information, manage risks and demonstrate operational credibility.

“Outsourcing goes beyond simply outsourcing business functions or operations. It is about trust because companies open up their confidential information, business secrets and sensitive details to outsourcing providers,” Varanasi said.

He said companies that build strong compliance systems around labour practices, cybersecurity, data protection and governance would be better positioned to attract international clients.

“Compliance can serve as a platform for strategic advantage,” he said.

Managing Partner at MP Olaniwun Ajayi LP, Tominiyi Owolabi, said data protection has become a major issue for outsourcing companies as regulators and global businesses increase scrutiny over how personal and corporate information is handled.

He said companies must demonstrate that they have proper systems for transferring, processing and protecting sensitive data.

“Companies that ensure they have proper processes in place to secure client assets, business secrets and personal data are positioning themselves better to attract clients,” he said.

He added that regulatory excellence should go beyond meeting minimum requirements.

“Regulatory compliance is often seen as a negative thing, but regulatory excellence, which goes beyond simply being qualified, is a positive thing to have in place,” he said.

Group Head, Outsource Services at Sterling Bank, Eke Ewang, highlighted the need for outsourcing firms and client organisations to improve employee experience, inclusion and welfare.

He said outsourced workers should not be treated differently from permanent employees, arguing that recognition, access to development opportunities and better engagement would improve productivity and retention.

The panel also stressed that stronger collaboration among regulators, outsourcing providers and businesses would be critical to creating a sustainable ecosystem capable of competing globally.

For Nigeria, industry leaders said the opportunity lies in converting its large workforce into a globally competitive talent pool, but that will require investment in skills, stronger regulation and trust-based business practices.
